title: Attention Is All You Need: how the Transformer became the foundation of every large model
summary: ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini are all built on the Transformer. This 2017 paper threw out recurrence and used attention alone to process language. We take it apart piece by piece—problem, formulas, experiments—with worked examples and quiz questions, so by the end you can explain for yourself why it works.
ai_summary: In 2017, researchers at Google proposed the Transformer at NIPS: instead of processing a sentence word by word in order, it lets every word attend to the whole sentence at once through attention. The core pieces are scaled dot-product attention (dividing by √dₖ to prevent softmax saturation), multi-head attention with 8 heads, sinusoidal positional encoding, and stacked encoder/decoder structures with 6 layers each. English-to-German translation reached 28.4 BLEU, more than 2 points above the previous best, after training for only 3.5 days on 8 GPUs. Limitations: compute grows quadratically with sequence length, and generation is still word by word; the English-to-French score appears as 41.8 in the abstract but 41.0 in the main text.
brief: The problem: recurrent networks must compute one word at a time, so they cannot be parallelized, and information between distant words has to be passed along step by step.

The method: attention only. Each word uses a query to match against every word's keys, then retrieves their values by weight; 8 heads each look at different things, and sinusoidal positional encoding adds word order back.
The result: 28.4 BLEU on English-to-German, more than 2 points above the previous best, including ensembles; the base model trains at a fraction of the cost of its competitors.
The impact: GPT, BERT, and today's large language models are all built on this architecture; the quadratic compute cost it left behind remains an active research problem.

paper.title: Attention Is All You Need
paper.authors: Ashish Vaswani, Noam Shazeer, Niki Parmar, Jakob Uszkoreit, Llion Jones, Aidan N. Gomez, Łukasz Kaiser, Illia Polosukhin
paper.org: Google Brain · Google Research · University of Toronto

cover.headline: A close reading of the original Transformer paper
cover.highlight: How attention alone reads a sentence

sections.h: The bottom line: what the paper actually did

blocks.p: In 2017, eight researchers from Google Brain, Google Research, and the University of Toronto published this paper—just 10 pages of main text—at NIPS 2017. It proposed a neural network architecture called **Transformer**: when processing a sentence, it no longer reads word by word in order, but lets every word look across the entire sentence at once, then decides which other words to focus on and how much. That mechanism—who to look at, and how much—is called **attention**.

The problem the paper set out to solve was concrete: machine translation. The results were just as concrete: 28.4 BLEU on English-to-German, more than 2 points above the previous best, including multi-model ensembles; and the largest model trained in 3.5 days on a single machine with 8 P100 GPUs.

But its impact goes far beyond translation. Today's ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini are all variants of the Transformer at their core—the T in GPT stands for Transformer. So understanding this paper is the key to understanding every large model. Below, we start with the problem it set out to solve, then dismantle it piece by piece and put it back together.

callout.title: The one-sentence version
callout.text: Transformer = attention (each word looks across the whole sentence and pulls in information by relevance) + feed-forward network (each word processes that information in place) + positional encoding (adds word order back) + residual connections and layer normalization (so stacking many layers still trains), with that layer repeated 6 times.

callout.title: Three small concepts you'll need
callout.text: Don't worry if you don't know them yet—these three are enough:
list: **Vector**: a list of numbers. The model represents a word's meaning as a list of numbers, and words with similar meanings have similar numbers.

**Dot product**: multiply two lists of numbers position by position and add the results. The more two vectors point in the same direction, the larger the dot product—roughly, the more similar they are.
**Softmax**: turns a set of scores into a set of proportions that add up to 1, with higher scores getting larger proportions.

sections.h: Before the Transformer: why word-by-word reading hit a wall

blocks.p: Before 2017, the mainstream translation model was the **recurrent neural network** (RNN, and its improved cousins LSTM and GRU). It reads a sentence the way a person reads with a finger under the words: at word t, you hold one memory hₜ, computed from the previous memory hₜ₋₁ and the current word.

The paper points to the fundamental problem: **each step must wait for the previous one to finish before it can start**. You cannot parallelize within a single sentence, and longer sentences take longer to process; once sentences get long, memory limits how many can be packed together. GPUs excel at doing many identical calculations at once—RNNs force them to work in a queue.

The second problem is that long-distance information must be passed along like a relay. A subject at the start of a sentence can't influence a verb at the end without the signal passing through every intermediate word's memory—and the farther it travels, the more it degrades. The paper captures this with **path length**: in an RNN, positions n words apart are O(n) steps away.

Some models used convolutional networks to get parallelism (the paper compares ConvS2S and ByteNet), but a single convolutional layer only sees a few neighboring words. To connect distant words you need many layers: ConvS2S's path length grows linearly with distance, ByteNet's grows logarithmically.

Attention had been around since 2014, but almost always as an accessory to RNNs. This paper asked a bold question: what if you throw out recurrence and convolution and keep **only attention**? The title "Attention Is All You Need" is their answer.

sections.h: What attention is: a weighted lookup

callout.title: Think of attention as a trip to the library to look something up.
callout.text: You walk into a library with a question (**Query**). Every book has a label on its spine (**Key**), and the book itself holds the actual content (**Value**). You compare your question with each label; the more relevant the book, the more attention it gets. The answer you come away with is the content of all the books weighted by how relevant each one is. In the Transformer, every word plays all three roles at once: the questioner, the label being compared, and the content being retrieved.

blocks.p: The paper defines attention in a single sentence: map a query and a set of key-value pairs to an output; the output is a weighted sum of the values, where each value's weight is determined by how well the query matches its key. The specific algorithm is **scaled dot-product attention**, written as:

formula.expr: Attention(Q, K, V) = softmax( Q·Kᵀ / √dₖ ) · V

parts.desc: Query matrix—each row is what a word is looking for
Key matrix—each row is the label by which a word can be found
Value matrix—each row is the information a word actually carries
Dot every query with every key to get a table of scores for who is related to whom, and how much
Square root of the key vector length dₖ; it shrinks the scores, for reasons explained in the next section
Turn each row of the score table into weights that add up to 1
Use those weights to average the values of all words, producing each word's new representation

formula.note: The whole process is just two matrix multiplications and one softmax—exactly the operations GPUs are best at—so an entire sentence can be computed at once.

blocks.p: Where do Q, K, and V come from? Each word is first represented as a 512-dimensional vector (d_{model} = 512 in the paper), then multiplied by three learned matrices W^{Q}, W^{K}, and W^{V} to produce its query, key, and value. Those three matrices are learned during training: the model figures out for itself what each word should ask, what label it should show, and what content it should hand over.
Let's hand-compute a tiny example. Suppose the sentence is "cat sat on the mat," and now "cat" does the query. Vector length dₖ = 4. To keep the math easy, the numbers are made up:

fig.title: Hand-computing attention: "cat" pays most attention to itself, then to "the mat"
fig.subtitle: Illustrative: vectors are invented for demonstration, not from the paper. Query q = [1, 0, 1, 0], dₖ = 4, so √dₖ = 2.
fig.note: Output = 0.506 × [10, 0] + 0.186 × [0, 10] + 0.307 × [5, 5] ≈ [6.6, 3.4]. In the new representation for "cat," its own information accounts for more than half, with a fair amount of "the mat" mixed in.

blocks.p: Notice two things. First, the weights are **relative**: softmax cares only about the differences between scores, not their absolute size. Second, the output is a **blend**: the new vector for "cat" no longer represents just a cat, but "the cat that sat on the mat in this sentence." Layer after layer of this blending makes each word's representation more context-aware.

callout.title: Attention is not just about highlighting a few words
callout.text: Many people think attention just highlights the important words. It is actually a continuous weighted average: every word in the sentence is seen, just with larger or smaller weights—and those weights are not hand-written rules, but learned from training data.

sections.h: Why divide by √dₖ: an easy-to-miss detail that matters

blocks.p: The √dₖ in the formula looks like a casually added constant, but the paper devotes a footnote to it—and it is key to understanding why attention is trainable at all.

The paper's derivation goes like this: suppose each component of query q and key k is an independent random variable with mean 0 and variance 1. Then their dot product q·k = q₁k₁ + q₂k₂ + … + q_{dₖ}k_{dₖ} is the sum of dₖ random terms, still with mean 0 but with **variance dₖ**. With dₖ = 64 in each head, the dot product's standard deviation is √64 = 8, so scores routinely land in the teens or twenties.
When scores swing wide, softmax becomes extreme: the largest score takes nearly all the weight, and the rest approach 0. See the comparison below:

fig.title: Same relative differences, scaled 8×: softmax gives almost all weight to the top score
fig.subtitle: Illustrative calculation: the three scores have the same relative ratios; the second row is multiplied by 8.

blocks.p: When weights are flattened to near 0 and 1, softmax sits in a **tiny gradient** region: no matter how the model nudges its parameters, the output barely changes, so it gets no signal about which direction to update. Training stalls. Dividing by √dₖ pulls the dot-product variance back to 1 and keeps softmax in a learnable range.

The paper also compares with another common form, "additive attention" (which uses a small neural network to compute compatibility). For large dₖ, additive attention outperforms **unscaled** dot-product attention; with scaling added, dot-product attention is both fast—because it can use highly optimized matrix multiplication—and no worse in quality.

quiz.q: If you increase each head's dₖ from 64 to 256 but still divide by 8 (i.e., keep scaling by √64), what is the most likely problem?
options: Less computation, faster training
Dot-product variance becomes 4× larger, softmax becomes more extreme, gradients shrink, and training gets harder
No effect—softmax only sees relative score differences
Attention becomes more uniform, with all words weighted about equally
quiz.why: According to the paper's footnote, dot-product variance equals dₖ. When dₖ goes from 64 to 256, variance grows by a factor of 4, and the standard deviation goes from 8 to 16. If you still divide by only 8, the scores are twice as large as before, so softmax is more easily flattened. The correct fix is to divide by √256 = 16. Option C is only half right: softmax does only see relative differences, but scaling all scores up also magnifies those differences.

sections.h: Multi-head attention: eight "experts" each look at different things

blocks.p: A single attention operation has a flaw: each word ends up with a weighted **average**, and averaging mixes different kinds of relationships together. The word "it," for example, needs to know both what it refers to (a coreference relation) and what role it plays in the sentence (a syntactic relation)—one average can't hold both at once. The paper's wording: with a single head, averaging inhibits this.

The paper's solution is **multi-head attention**: split the 512 dimensions into 8 slices of 64 (h = 8, dₖ = dᵥ = 64). Each slice runs attention independently with its own W^{Q}, W^{K}, W^{V}; the 8 results are concatenated back to 512 dimensions and multiplied by a matrix W^{O} to blend them. Because each head works at one-eighth the full dimension, total computation is similar to a full-size single head—like getting 7 extra experts for free.

formula.expr:
MultiHead(Q, K, V) = Concat(head₁, …, head₈) · W^{O}
headᵢ = Attention(Q·W_{i}^{Q}, K·W_{i}^{K}, V·W_{i}^{V})

parts.desc: Head i: project Q, K, V down to 64 dimensions with its own matrices, then run scaled dot-product attention.
Concatenate the eight 64-dimensional outputs back into 8 × 64 = 512 dimensions.
Then multiply by a matrix to fuse the eight experts' opinions into one result.

fig.title: Two heads looking differently: Head 1 tracks what "it" refers to, Head 2 tracks the immediately preceding word
fig.subtitle: Illustrative: numbers are examples, not from the paper. Each row is one word's attention distribution and sums to about 1; darker amber means more weight, and the amber outline marks the row for "it."
fig.note: Head 1: when reading "it," most attention lands on "cat," so the model infers that "it" refers to the cat (the hungry one is the cat, not the mouse).

fig.title: Head 2 uses a different focus: almost every word attends to the word immediately before it
fig.subtitle: Illustrative: numbers are examples, not from the paper.

blocks.p: This isn't wishful thinking. The paper's appendix visualizes the attention of trained heads: in encoder layer 5, some heads reach across long distances, linking the verb "making" with the later phrase "more difficult"; two heads specialize in coreference, concentrating on "Law" when reading "its"; others clearly follow sentence structure. The paper's conclusion: different heads really do learn different jobs.

fig.title: Too few or too many heads hurt: 8 or 16 heads are best
fig.subtitle: Unit: BLEU, English-to-German dev set (newstest2013), with total computation held constant. Amber marks the paper's default of 8 heads.
fig.note: From group (A) of Table 3 in the paper: more heads means fewer dimensions per head.

blocks.p: A single head scores 0.9 BLEU below the best setting; but more heads isn't always better. With 32 heads, each head gets only 16 dimensions—too little capacity—and the score falls back to 25.4. 0.9 may not sound like much, but remember that this paper's record-breaking margin was only about 2 points.

sections.h: No order: how the model knows word order—positional encoding

blocks.p: Attention has a built-in blind spot: it **has no idea of order**. When each word looks at the whole sentence, it sees a pile of words and their meanings, with no information about which came first. Without intervention, "dog bites man" and "man bites dog" look like the same three words—nearly impossible to tell apart. RNNs don't have this problem because they read in order; once you throw out recurrence, you need another way to put order back in.

The paper's solution is to create a "position vector" for each position and **add** it to the word vector (both are 512-dimensional, so they can be summed). The position vectors are generated from sine and cosine functions of different frequencies:

formula.expr:
PE(pos, 2i) = sin( pos / 10000^{2i/d_{model}} )
PE(pos, 2i+1) = cos( pos / 10000^{2i/d_{model}} )

parts.desc: The word's position in the sentence: 0, 1, 2, ...
Dimension index. Even dimensions use sin, odd dimensions use cos, in pairs.
Controls the slowest wave: wavelengths stretch from 2π to 10000·2π.

callout.title: Like a clock with many hands
callout.text: The second hand spins fast, the minute hand slower, and the hour hand slower still. Looking only at the second hand, you can't tell 1 o'clock from 2 o'clock; combine the positions of several hands and a moment is uniquely determined. The 512 dimensions of the positional encoding are like 256 pairs of faster and slower hands (each pair has one sin and one cos), so every position gets a unique set of "hand readings."

blocks.p: Why sine and cosine specifically? The paper's reason is that, for any fixed offset k, the encoding at position pos + k can be written as a **linear function** of the encoding at position pos (the trigonometric sum identities guarantee this). That makes it easy for the model to learn relative-position relationships such as "look three words ahead."

The paper also tried another approach: instead of using a formula, let the model learn a vector for each position. The results were almost identical (dev set BLEU 25.7 vs. 25.8). It chose the sinusoidal version because it may let the model handle sentences longer than those seen during training, since the formula can compute an encoding for any position.

quiz.q: If positional encoding were removed entirely, what capability would the Transformer lose most directly?
options: It would lose the ability to compute in parallel.
It would be unable to distinguish word order; "dog bites man" and "man bites dog" would be hard to tell apart.
It would be unable to process sentences longer than 512 words.
It would be unable to do multi-head attention.
quiz.why: Attention itself is insensitive to order; word-order information comes entirely from positional encoding. Parallelism comes from the structure of attention, not from positional encoding, and multi-head attention still computes fine—it just wouldn't know which word came first.

sections.h: Putting the pieces together: 6 encoder layers, 6 decoder layers

blocks.p: Like the mainstream translation models of its time, the Transformer is split into two halves: the **encoder** reads the source text (say, an English sentence) and turns each word into a context-aware vector; the **decoder** uses those vectors to write the translation (say, in German) one word at a time, treating the words already written as input for the next one. Both sides stack the same layer structure 6 times (N = 6).

fig.title: Four steps inside one encoder layer
fig.subtitle: Illustrative: every step outputs 512 dimensions, so the outputs can be added and layers can be stacked.

steps.name: Multi-head self-attention
steps.desc: Each word looks across the whole sentence and mixes in information from the other words by relevance.

steps.name: Residual + layer norm
steps.desc: Adds the result of this step back to the original input, then pulls the values back into a stable range.

steps.name: Feed-forward network
steps.desc: Each word goes through a small two-layer network on its own, with ReLU in the middle, processing the information it has just gathered in place.

steps.name: Residual + layer norm
steps.desc: Again add to the input, normalize, then pass the result to the next layer.

parts.desc: Expands the 512-dimensional word vector to 2048 dimensions.
ReLU: negative values become 0, positive values stay unchanged. This adds nonlinearity to the network.
Then compresses it back to 512 dimensions.

formula.note: Every position uses the same parameters, but different layers have different parameters. The paper notes this can also be seen as two convolutions with kernel size 1.

blocks.p: **Residual connection** means "copy the input as-is and add it to the output." That way each layer only has to learn how much to change from its input, and signals and gradients can travel straight through many layers along this shortcut, avoiding the training problems that come with depth. It comes from ResNet in 2015, which this paper cites. **Layer normalization** then pulls the values of each word vector back to around mean 0 and variance 1, making training more stable.
Each decoder layer has one more sublayer than an encoder layer, three in total:

list: **Masked self-attention**: the words in the target sentence can only see themselves and the words before them; they can't peek at words later. The trick is to set the scores of future positions to negative infinity before the softmax, so after softmax those positions get weight 0.

**Encoder–decoder attention**: queries come from the decoder, and keys and values come from the encoder's output. In other words, every time it writes a German word, it checks back against the entire English source sentence.
**Feed-forward network**: the same as in the encoder.

callout.title: Masking is like covering the answers during an exam
callout.text: During training, the entire correct translation is fed in at once, so all positions can be computed in parallel; but each position has the later content masked out and can only predict the next word from the preceding words, simulating the real process of thinking while writing. This is exactly the mechanism today's large language models use to generate text.

callout.title: The Transformer is not just attention
callout.text: Counting the parameters in one layer at the paper's sizes: the four attention projection matrices (W^{Q}, W^{K}, W^{V}, W^{O}) have 4 × 512 × 512 parameters together, and the feed-forward network has 2 × 512 × 2048 parameters—exactly twice as many (ignoring biases). That means about two-thirds of the parameters in each layer sit in the feed-forward network. Attention moves information among words; the feed-forward network processes each word in place. Both are essential.

blocks.p: Two final small design choices: the input and output share the same embedding matrix (the encoder embeddings, the decoder embeddings, and the output layer that maps vectors back to words all use the same matrix), and the embeddings are multiplied by √d_{model} before the positional encoding is added.

sections.h: Why self-attention is better: the paper's three yardsticks

blocks.p: Section 4 of the paper is devoted to the question "why self-attention," and it uses three yardsticks: per-layer **computational cost**, how much computation can be parallelized (the minimum number of sequential steps required), and the **longest path** between any two positions. The comparison table earlier already gave the conclusion: self-attention connects any two words in a constant number of steps—the shortest path—and is the most suitable for parallelization.

The computational cost deserves a closer look. Self-attention costs n²·d per layer (n words compared pairwise, with each comparison d dimensions), while a recurrent layer costs n·d². Which is cheaper depends on whether the sentence length n or the vector dimension d is larger:

fig.title: When the sentence is shorter than the vector dimension, self-attention is cheaper; once sentences get long, it becomes much more expensive
fig.subtitle: Illustrative estimate: d = 512, comparing only the order of magnitude of per-layer computation.

blocks.p: The paper notes that in the translation tasks of its time, sentences represented as subwords were usually much shorter than 512, so self-attention was faster. But it also clearly saw the other side: for very long sequences, you can let each word attend only to the r nearest words (restricted self-attention), at the cost of increasing the maximum path length to O(n/r), and it lists this as future work. That n² problem later became the core challenge for the entire long-context research direction.

The paper also mentions a side benefit: attention weights can be inspected, which makes the model easier to interpret. The "who is attending to whom" diagrams in the previous section are drawn exactly this way.

quiz.q: According to the table above, when processing a long document of 4,000 subwords, the per-layer computation of self-attention is roughly how many times that of a recurrent layer?
options: About 0.1×
About the same
About 8×
About 512×
quiz.why: The ratio of n²·d to n·d² is n / d = 4000 / 512 ≈ 7.8. Whenever the sentence length exceeds the vector dimension, self-attention is more expensive, and each time the length doubles, its computation quadruples.

sections.h: How it was trained: 8 GPUs, 12 hours to 3.5 days

list: **Data**: English-to-German used the WMT 2014 dataset, about 4.5 million sentence pairs, segmented into subwords with byte-pair encoding (BPE), with a shared English-German vocabulary of about 37,000 subwords. English-to-French used a larger dataset of 36 million sentences with a vocabulary of 32,000 subwords. Each training batch contained about 25,000 source subwords and 25,000 target subwords.

**Hardware and duration**: one machine with 8 NVIDIA P100 GPUs. The base model took about 0.4 seconds per step and trained for 100,000 steps, 12 hours in total; the large model took 1.0 seconds per step and trained for 300,000 steps, 3.5 days in total.
**Regularization**: dropout was applied to each sublayer's output before it was added to the residual path, with a rate of 0.1 for the base model; label smoothing of 0.1 was also used.

blocks.p: The learning-rate schedule is designed with care. The paper gives this formula:

formula.expr: lrate = d_{model}^{−0.5} · min( step^{−0.5}, step · warmup^{−1.5} )

parts.desc: Warm-up step count; the paper uses 4000

For the first 4000 steps, the second term applies and the learning rate rises linearly with the step number; after that, the first term applies and the learning rate decreases slowly as the inverse square root of the step number.

callout.title: Why warm up?
callout.text: At the start of training the parameters are random and the model has no idea which direction it should go. Taking big steps right away can easily make it stumble (the loss oscillates sharply or even diverges). So it takes small steps first and gradually speeds up, then slowly reduces its stride once the direction stabilizes. This "rise then fall" learning-rate curve later became almost standard practice for training Transformers.

callout.title: Label smoothing: deliberately keeping the model from being too confident
callout.text: During training, the model is not asked to give the correct word a perfect score; instead, it leaves a little probability for the other words (the paper uses 0.1). The paper says this makes perplexity (a measure of how "certain" the model is) worse, because the model learns to be less sure, but final accuracy and BLEU both improve.

blocks.p: At test time there are a few more tricks: the base model averages the parameters of the last 5 checkpoints, and the large model averages the last 20. Translation uses beam search with beam size 4 and length penalty α = 0.6, considering several candidate translations at once instead of only picking the best current word at each step.

sections.h: The report card: better, and far cheaper

callout.title: What is BLEU?
callout.text: The most common automatic score for machine translation. It compares the machine translation with one or more human reference translations and counts how many words and phrases overlap. The maximum score is 100, and higher is better. A gap of a few points is already considered a notable improvement in this field.

fig.title: English-to-German: the Transformer base model already beats every previous model, including ensembles
fig.subtitle: Unit: BLEU, WMT 2014 English-to-German test set (newstest2014). Amber marks the Transformer.
fig.note: From Table 2 of the paper. Ensembling combines the results of multiple models; it usually outperforms a single model, but the cost multiplies accordingly.

fig.title: Training cost: the Transformer base model uses only a fraction of its competitors' compute
fig.subtitle: Unit: ×10¹⁸ FLOPs (English-to-German). Amber marks the Transformer; the paper estimates cost as training time × number of GPUs × per-GPU compute.
fig.note: For example, 23 means 2.3×10¹⁹. The base model costs about one-third of ConvS2S, yet scores more than 2 BLEU higher.

blocks.p: On English-to-German, the large model reaches 28.4 BLEU, more than 2 points above the previous best result (ConvS2S ensemble at 26.36); even the base model (27.3) beats every previously published model and ensemble.

On English-to-French, the abstract and Table 2 report 41.8 BLEU, a new single-model record; but Section 6.1 of the main text says 41.0. The two numbers are inconsistent, and the paper doesn't explain the discrepancy—worth noting when you read it, and when citing it's best to follow the table and mention the inconsistency. The paper also says its training cost is under one-quarter of the previous best model.

To prove the Transformer isn't only good at translation, the authors also applied it to **English constituency parsing**: they write a sentence's parse tree as a string of symbols and let the model "translate" it. This task has outputs much longer than inputs and very strong structural constraints. With only about 40,000 sentences from the Wall Street Journal as training data, a 4-layer Transformer scored 91.3 F1; with added semi-supervised data it reached 92.7, surpassing all previous methods except one specially designed grammar model (RNNG, 93.3), with almost no task-specific tuning.

sections.h: Ablation experiments: which design choices actually matter

blocks.p: Table 3 of the paper runs a set of "control variable" experiments: each time, only one part of the base model is changed, and the score on the English-to-German dev set shows the effect. This is the most reliable way to judge which design choice is really critical.

fig.title: Change one thing at a time and watch how the score moves
fig.subtitle: From Table 3 of the paper, English-to-German dev set (newstest2013); the base model has a BLEU of 25.8 and 65 million parameters. The amber column is BLEU.
rows: Keys too short; judging who relates to whom gets harder
Almost identical to the sinusoidal version

blocks.p: Four conclusions emerge from this table: multiple heads do help, but the number should be moderate; too small a dₖ hurts quality, and the paper speculates from this that judging compatibility is not simple—a more complex matching function than the dot product might be better; larger models are better; and dropout is very important for preventing overfitting.

callout.title: How to read an ablation table
callout.text: When a paper introduces several new designs, ablation experiments tell you how much each design contributes. When you read a paper, checking the ablation table first often says more about the paper's true contribution than the final results do.

sections.h: What it didn't solve—and what happened next

blocks.p: The paper ends by candidly listing what to do next, and those next steps happened to become the main storylines of AI development over the following years:

list: **Long sequences are expensive**: self-attention's compute grows quadratically with sequence length. The paper suggests letting each word attend only locally; the later sparse attention, efficient attention, and long-context techniques all wrestle with this n².

**Generation is still sequential**: the decoder still writes one word at a time. The paper lists making generation less dependent on order as a research goal; today large models still generate text word by word, and inference acceleration remains a hot area.

**Extending beyond text**: the paper plans to use the Transformer on images, audio, and video. A few years later, Vision Transformer (2020) cut images into patches and treated them as words, and the diffusion model DiT (2022) also moved to the Transformer.

blocks.p: The Transformer's encoder and decoder were later split apart and developed separately: the encoder-only BERT (2018) excels at understanding, and the decoder-only GPT series excels at generation. Today's large language models mostly use only the decoder half, and they have improved details such as where normalization is placed and how position is encoded, but the "attention + feed-forward + residual" skeleton remains exactly the one in this paper.

callout.title: What to read next
callout.text: These follow-up papers are all on our reading list: BERT, GPT-3, Vision Transformer, Scaling Laws... They will each be explained thoroughly, and completed ones will appear on the close-reading page.

sections.h: Check yourself: have you really absorbed it?

quiz.q: What is the most fundamental reason the Transformer can train much faster than an RNN?
options: Fewer parameters
All positions in the same sentence can be computed simultaneously, without waiting for the previous word
Better GPUs
Removing positional encoding
quiz.why: Step t of an RNN depends on the result of step t−1, so the computation can only run in sequence. With self-attention, every word directly sees the whole sentence, so the entire sentence can be processed with matrix multiplication in a single pass, making full use of GPU parallelism. The paper's base model has 65 million parameters, which is not small.

quiz.q: In the decoder's "encoder–decoder attention," where do the query (Q), key (K), and value (V) come from?
options: Q, K, and V all come from the encoder
Q comes from the decoder; K and V come from the encoder's output
Q comes from the encoder; K and V come from the decoder
Q, K, and V all come from the decoder
quiz.why: The decoder uses its own current state to ask the question (Q), then looks up the encoder's representation of the source in the keys and values (K, V). This is the step where every word being written checks back against the original text.

quiz.q: Why does the decoder's self-attention need masking?
options: To reduce computation
To prevent the model from peeking at the correct answer at later positions when predicting a given position
To make attention more uniform
To replace positional encoding
quiz.why: During training, the entire target sentence is fed in at once. If later words were not masked, the model could copy the answer directly and would never learn true word-by-word generation. Masking sets the scores of future positions to negative infinity, so after softmax their weights become 0.

callout.title: After reading, you should be able to answer these five questions in your own words
list: Why is an RNN slow, and why can self-attention be parallelized?
What are Q, K, and V, and how is a single attention computation carried out?
Why divide by √dₖ? What happens if you don't?
What problem of single-head attention does multi-head attention solve?
Without recurrence, how does the model know the order of words?
